platforms.title: Jawline Acne Past 20 Is Usually About Diet, Not Cleansing
platforms.meta_description: Still breaking out along your jaw past 20? The cause might be diet, not skincare — blood sugar spikes raise a hormone called IGF-1 that ramps up oil production.
platforms.body_html:
If you're well past 20 and still breaking out along your jaw and cheeks, the first thing worth questioning isn't your cleanser or your skincare routine — it's what you ate that day. Repeated spikes and crashes in blood sugar push things in the direction of more acne, and the signal starts inside the body, not on the surface of the skin.

The Hormone That Links Blood Sugar to Breakouts

Meals high in refined carbs and sugar send blood glucose up quickly, and insulin follows to bring it back down. That process also raises a hormone called IGF-1 (insulin-like growth factor 1), and dermatology research links elevated IGF-1 to increased oil production and thickened skin cells around pores. More oil plus thicker, flakier skin around the pore opening makes clogging more likely, and clogged pores that develop inflammation are exactly what becomes acne.

What Actually Helps Once You Know Which Three Foods Trigger It

A daily plate built around refined carbs like white rice or white bread is the most common starting point — it digests fast, so blood sugar spikes quickly and insulin and IGF-1 swing hard right along with it. Dairy, even something like plain Greek yogurt chosen as a "healthy" option, isn't exempt either. Research has linked dairy intake to elevated IGF-1 and androgen receptor activity independent of sugar content, and studies comparing people with and without adult acne have found higher circulating IGF-1 in the acne group. Fried food and pastries pile inflammation on top of that. High-heat frying generates trans fats and oxidative byproducts, and these foods are usually loaded with sugar too — which lines up with research linking high-glycemic diets to greater acne risk.

Swapping half your white rice for brown rice or oats slows the glucose spike, which softens the insulin and IGF-1 swing that follows. Switching Greek yogurt for a plant-based alternative, or simply eating less of it, is worth trying. Air-frying sweet potato instead of reaching for a donut cuts out both the frying oil and a chunk of the added sugar. If changing all three feels like too much at once, start by recalling what you were eating during your worst recent breakout — that's usually the clearest clue.

It also helps to actually write down what you eat for a week or two, the same way food diaries work for other conditions — most people are surprised how often the same two or three foods show up right before a flare. Pay attention to how a breakout tracks with your cycle, stress levels, and sleep too, since IGF-1 and insulin sensitivity both shift with all three, and diet alone rarely explains everything happening on your skin at once.

None of this clears skin overnight. Skin cells take weeks to turn over and hormone signals take time to settle, so give any dietary change at least a month before judging it. If breakouts are severe or leaving scars, see a dermatologist alongside any diet changes rather than instead of them.
